podcast.title: A Cappella Performance and Formalized Structure
podcast.body: This style of music was typically performed a cappella, though sometimes a single instrument might be added. It developed a relatively formalized structure with specific parts for tenor, soprano, alto, and bass, adhering to strict four-part harmony common in European choral music. The soprano and alto parts were sung in falsetto by men. "This new style of music was usually performed at Capella, though sometimes there might be a single instrument added, and it gained a relatively formalised structure."

podcast.title: Fusion of Musical Elements
podcast.body: Isekathamia combines elements of traditional Zulu music with two Western influences: religious music heard from church missions, and American minstrel songs, particularly those performed by troupes led by Orfius Macadoo that toured South Africa in the late 19th century. "Those people combined elements of traditional Zulu music with two more Western elements. The first was the religious music that they heard from church missions, and the second was American minstrel songs."

podcast.title: Origins in Forced Displacement
podcast.body: This music form was created when rural black people in South Africa were forcibly displaced in the late 19th century and compelled to find work in cities. "it's a music created when rural black people were forcibly displaced in the late 19th century and forced to find work in the city."

podcast.title: Western Chord Progressions and Zulu Language Adaptation
podcast.body: Isekathamia music usually centered around the common one, four, and five chords found in most Western popular music. The Zulu language lyrics were often distorted to fit Western meters, although the music maintained a more freeform quality compared to much of the Western music of that era. "It would usually be based around the same one four and five chords, that most Western popular music was based on, and the Zulu language would often be distorted to fit western metres, though the music was still more freeform than most of the Western music of the time."
